questions.title: Why an oral glucose load clears faster than an intravenous one
questions.question: One group of subjects is given 50 g of glucose intravenously and another 50 g orally. Which factor best explains why the oral glucose load is cleared from the blood faster than the intravenous load?

explanations.A: Incorrect. CCK is released by fat and protein, not by an oral glucose load, and it is not the incretin responsible for enhanced insulin secretion after oral glucose.
explanations.B: Incorrect. VIP is an enteric neurotransmitter causing smooth-muscle relaxation and secretion; it does not mediate the insulin response to oral glucose.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glucagon raises blood glucose and would slow clearance, so a glucagon-releasing action cannot explain faster clearance of oral glucose.
explanations.D: Correct. Oral glucose passes the gut and releases glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP) from duodenal K cells. GIP is an incretin that strongly potentiates glucose-stimulated insulin release from pancreatic beta cells. Because intravenous glucose bypasses the gut and releases no incretin, the oral load produces more insulin and is cleared faster — the incretin effect.

questions.learning_objective: Explain the incretin effect: oral glucose releases GIP, which augments insulin secretion, so oral glucose clears faster than intravenous glucose.

questions.title: How the cephalic phase of gastric secretion is abolished
questions.question: The cephalic phase of gastric secretion accounts for about 30 percent of the acid response to a meal. Which of the following can completely eliminate the cephalic phase?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and reduces vagally driven acid secretion, but it does not completely abolish the cephalic phase and has widespread anticholinergic effects.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An H2 blocker reduces histamine-mediated acid secretion but only blunts, rather than eliminates, the vagally mediated cephalic phase.
explanations.C: Correct. The cephalic phase — triggered by the sight, smell, taste and thought of food — is mediated entirely through the vagus nerve. Cutting the vagus (vagotomy) removes this efferent pathway. Therefore vagotomy can completely abolish the cephalic phase of gastric secretion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sympathetic system is generally inhibitory to gastric secretion, so sympathectomy would not eliminate the vagally driven cephalic phase.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cephalic phase of gastric secretion is mediated entirely by the vagus, so vagotomy abolishes it.

questions.title: Second messenger raised by cholera toxin in enterocytes
questions.question: After a community outbreak of Vibrio cholerae, the toxin acts on the intestinal crypt epithelial cells. It is most likely to cause an increase in which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. Cholera toxin irreversibly activates the stimulatory G protein (Gs) of adenylate cyclase in the enterocyte. This causes a sustained, irreversible rise in intracellular cAMP. The elevated cAMP then drives the secretory response responsible for the diarrhoea.
explanations.B: Incorrect. cGMP is the second messenger raised by the heat-stable enterotoxin of E. coli, not by cholera toxin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cholera toxin causes chloride secretion into the lumen, not chloride absorption.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The toxin impairs, rather than increases, sodium absorption; net secretion of ions and water is the result.

questions.title: Ion channel irreversibly opened in cholera
questions.question: In the same patients with cholera, which type of ion channel in the intestinal epithelial cells is most likely to be irreversibly opened?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Calcium channels are not the effector opened by the cholera-toxin/cAMP pathway.
explanations.B: Correct. The raised cAMP produced by cholera toxin phosphorylates and irreversibly opens the apical chloride channel (CFTR). Chloride pours into the lumen, sodium follows to preserve electroneutrality, and water follows the osmotic gradient. The result is the massive secretory diarrhoea of cholera.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Magnesium channels play no role in the cholera secretory mechanism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Although potassium is lost in the stool, the channel irreversibly opened by the toxin is the chloride (CFTR) channel, which is the primary driver of secretion.

questions.title: Fall in which mediator allows the post-prandial rise in acid secretion
questions.question: After a meal the gastric pH first rises, and a few minutes later the rate of acid secretion increases again. A decrease in which substance most likely facilitates this secondary increase in acid secretion?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gastrin stimulates acid secretion, so a decrease in gastrin would reduce, not increase, acid output.
explanations.B: Incorrect. CCK has essentially no physiological role in regulating gastric acid secretion in this setting.
explanations.C: Correct. When the stomach is empty and acidic, the low pH stimulates antral D cells to release somatostatin, which directly and indirectly (via suppression of gastrin) inhibits acid secretion. When a meal buffers the acid and raises the pH, somatostatin release falls. The removal of this paracrine brake allows the secondary rise in acid secretion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. VIP is not a physiological regulator of the post-prandial rise in gastric acid secretion.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that somatostatin is the paracrine brake on gastric acid; a fall in somatostatin after meal buffering permits the secondary acid rise.

questions.title: Forerunner mechanism of gastric ulcer formation
questions.question: A man is found to have a chronic gastric ulcer that has perforated toward the liver. Which mechanism is a forerunner to gastric ulcer formation?

options.A: Back-leak of hydrogen ions into the mucosa

explanations.A: Correct. When the gastric mucosal barrier is damaged, hydrogen ions leak back from the lumen into the mucosa. The intracellular buffers become saturated, cell pH falls, and injury with histamine release, capillary damage and focal ischaemia follows. This mucosal lesion is the forerunner of a gastric ulcer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mucus secretion strengthens and protects the mucosal barrier; it opposes ulcer formation rather than causing it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Proton pump inhibition reduces acid and is a treatment for ulcers, not a cause.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tight junctions between surface cells are part of the intact barrier that prevents acid back-leak; they protect against, rather than cause, ulceration.

questions.learning_objective: State that back-leak of hydrogen ions through a damaged gastric mucosal barrier is the forerunner of gastric ulcer formation.

questions.title: Mediator of receptive relaxation of the LES and fundus
questions.question: As a boy swallows, his lower oesophageal sphincter and gastric fundus relax while the food is still in the oesophagus. Which substance most likely mediates this relaxation?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gastrin has no significant effect on smooth-muscle relaxation at physiological levels and does not mediate receptive relaxation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Motilin drives the migrating motor complex between meals; it is not the mediator of receptive relaxation during swallowing.
explanations.C: Correct. Receptive relaxation (and the accompanying relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter and fundus) is a vagovagal reflex. The inhibitory enteric neurotransmitter released onto the smooth muscle is nitric oxide (with VIP). Nitric oxide therefore mediates the relaxation that accommodates the swallowed bolus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Norepinephrine is a sympathetic transmitter and is not involved in the vagally mediated receptive relaxation.

questions.learning_objective: State that nitric oxide is the inhibitory neurotransmitter that mediates receptive relaxation of the fundus and lower oesophageal sphincter.

questions.title: Hormone whose loss causes GI mucosal atrophy on intravenous feeding
questions.question: A man is fed intravenously for several weeks after a severe accident, and his gastrointestinal mucosa atrophies. This is most likely because the blood level of which hormone is reduced?

explanations.A: Incorrect. CCK stimulates growth of the exocrine pancreas rather than being the main trophic hormone for the gastrointestinal mucosa.
explanations.B: Correct. Gastrin has a critical trophic role, stimulating growth of the mucosa throughout the stomach and intestines. Intravenous feeding removes the luminal nutrients that normally release gastrin, so blood gastrin falls. The loss of this trophic drive leads to atrophy of the gastrointestinal mucosa.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Secretin stimulates pancreatic and biliary bicarbonate secretion and pancreatic growth, not general mucosal growth.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Although CCK is trophic to the pancreas, the mucosal atrophy of the gut is attributed to reduced gastrin, so the single best answer is gastrin only.

questions.learning_objective: State that gastrin is the main trophic hormone for the GI mucosa, so reduced gastrin during intravenous feeding causes mucosal atrophy.
